rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: The opening citations identify the man who bites his hands as ʿUqba ibn Abi Muʿayṭ and the one who regrets his friend as Umayya ibn Khalaf.
rows.anchor: قاله النحاس. والمعنى في نداء البشرى:

rows.speaker: سيبويه والسهيلي
rows.claim: Calling out “my good news” summons those present to share the news, more emphatically than saying “I rejoiced”; it resembles exclamations such as “what a wonder!”
rows.anchor: وهذا مذهب سيبويه، وكذا قال السهيلي. وقيل: هو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He prefers construing bushrā as the verbal noun of rejoicing, not a proper name: a proper name would not take the first-person possessive suffix; the vocative calls attention to joy.
rows.anchor: وهذا أصح لأنه لو كان اسما علما لم يكن مضافا إلى ضمير المتكلم

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: On al-Suddī’s analysis, bushrā is nominative, as in the vocative “O Zayd, this is a boy”; an accusative analysis is also possible.
rows.anchor: وعلى قول السدي يكون في موضع رفع كما تقول: يا زيد هذا غلام.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative accusative parses bushrā as an indefinite vocative, like the Qur’anic “O regret for the servants.”
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون محله نصبا كقولك: يا رجلا، وقوله:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “they concealed him as merchandise,” the pronoun refers to Joseph; the plural subject may be his brothers, the traders, or the water-drawer and his companions.
rows.anchor: الهاء كناية عن يوسف عليه السلام فأما الواو فكناية عن إخوته

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says Mālik ibn Daʿr and fellow traders hid Joseph as entrusted merchandise, claiming people of Syria or the well had consigned him, to prevent the caravan sharing him.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: أسره مالك بن دعر وأصحابه من التجار الذين معهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the brothers claimed Joseph was their runaway slave; Joseph agreed to the claim after they threatened to kill him, and they sold him.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: أسره إخوة يوسف بضاعة لما استخرج من الجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In a further account Judah advised Joseph to accept the brothers’ ownership claim to escape death; Mālik doubted he was a slave, but Joseph confirmed their account and Mālik bought him.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن يهوذا وصى أخاه يوسف بلسانهم أن اعترف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sharaytu can mean either “I bought” or “I sold”; the cited poems attest its use for selling.
rows.anchor: يقال: شريت بمعنى اشتريت، وشريت بمعنى بعت لغة قال الشاعر:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bakhṣ means a reduced or deficient price; the brothers wanted Joseph removed from their father’s attention, not profit from the sale.
rows.anchor: أي نقص وهو هنا مصدر وضع موضع الاسم أي باعوه بثمن مبخوس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account says Judah saw Joseph emerge from the well and alerted the brothers; another says they returned three days later, followed the caravan, claimed Joseph as a runaway, and sold him.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن يهوذا رأى من بعيد أن يوسف أخرج من الجب فأخبر إخوته

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda glosses bakhṣ as “wrongful.”
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: «بخس» ظلم.

rows.speaker: الضحاك ومقاتل والسدي وابن عطاء
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Muqātil, al-Suddī, and Ibn ʿAṭāʾ gloss bakhṣ as unlawful, though Ibn al-ʿArabī disputes this.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك ومقاتل والسدي وابن عطاء: «بخس» حرام.

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabī says bakhṣ means the price did not reach Joseph’s value, since the sellers sought separation from Jacob or concealed their profit, not a fair sale.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن العربي: ولا وجه له، وإنما الإشارة فيه إلى أنه لم يستوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author counters that full market payment would not make selling a free person lawful; the sale itself was invalid, so its price was unlawful, supporting al-Suddī and others.
rows.anchor: فدل على صحة ما قاله السدي وغيره لأنهم أوقعوا البيع على نفس لا يجوز بيعها

rows.speaker: عكرمة والشعبي وابن حيان
rows.claim: ʿIkrima and al-Shaʿbī gloss bakhṣ as “little”; Ibn Ḥayyān says it means counterfeit.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة والشعبي: قليل. وقال ابن حيان: زيف.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وابن مسعود
rows.claim: Reports from Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd give twenty dirhams, two for each of ten brothers; other reports give twenty-two for eleven brothers or forty, and the author prefers the Companion reports.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس وابن مسعود باعوه بعشرين درهما أخذ كل واحد من إخوته درهمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dirāhim is an appositive explanation of the price, and bakhṣ is an adjective of thaman; the morphology and count indicate a small sale.
rows.anchor: و «بخس» من نعت «ثمن». { دراهم } على البدل والتفسير له.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited line uses the plural form darāhīm; “counted” suggests coins were counted rather than weighed, or simply indicates a sum too small to require weighing.
rows.anchor: وهذا يدل على أن الأثمان كانت تجري عندهم عدا لا وزنا بوزن

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabī says gold and silver are fundamentally exchanged by equal weight, citing the Prophetic prohibition on unequal precious-metal exchange; counting was a practical convenience, while shortage restores weighing and coin clipping corrupts.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي ابن العربي: وأصل النقدين الوزن قال صلى الله عليه وسلم:

rows.speaker: أشهب وأبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Ashhab’s transmitted position, apparently Mālik’s view, and Abū Ḥanīfa’s hold that named dirhams and dinars do not become individually specified in the sale; they remain debts owed.
rows.anchor: فذهب أشهب إلى أن ذلك لا يتعين، وهو الظاهر من قول مالك وبه قال أبو حنيفة.

rows.speaker: ابن القاسم والشافعي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Qāsim and al-Shāfiʿī hold that the particular coins are specified; if they perish, the exchange contract lapses rather than creating replacement debts.
rows.anchor: وذهب ابن القاسم إلى أنها تتعين، وحكي عن الكرخي وبه قال الشافعي.

rows.speaker: الحسن بن علي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī reportedly ruled that a foundling is free and recited this verse as evidence; the author says the issue was discussed earlier.
rows.anchor: روي عن الحسن بن علي رضي الله عنهما أنه قضى في اللقيط أنه حر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “They were among those who cared little for him” may refer to the brothers, caravan, or water-drawer; each group wanted quick separation or sole possession, not Joseph’s worth.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: { وكانوا فيه من الزاهدين } قيل: المراد إخوته. وقيل:

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik holds that a binding sale may stand even when a valuable object is sold cheaply: a seller who mistakes a costly pearl for a worthless bead cannot undo the sale.
rows.anchor: ولهذا قال مالك: لو باع درة ذات خطر عظيم بدرهم ثم قال لم أعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations take their lack of desire to concern Joseph’s beauty or their ignorance of his standing with God; Sibawayh and al-Kisāʾī report both vowelings of zahida.
rows.anchor: وقيل: «وكانوا فيه من الزاهدين» لم يعلموا منزلته عند الله تعالى.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading takes ishtarā here as “took in exchange,” not a formal sale; another says the wording reflects how the transaction appeared to observers.
rows.anchor: قيل: الاشتراء هنا بمعنى الاستبدال إذ لم يكن ذلك عقدا، مثل:

rows.speaker: الضحاك والسهيلي
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk identifies the purchaser as Egypt’s king, titled al-ʿAzīz; al-Suhaylī gives his name as Quṭayfir.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك: هذا الذي اشتراه ملك مصر، ولقبه العزيز. السهيلي: واسمه قطفير.

rows.speaker: ابن إسحق
rows.claim: Ibn Isḥāq calls the purchaser Iṭfīr ibn Ruwayḥib and his wife Rāʿīl; another report names her Zulaykhā, with both names related by al-Thaʿlabī and others.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن إسحق: إطفير بن رويحب اشتراه لامرأته راعيل

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: Al-Qushayrī reports that God placed love of Joseph in the ʿAzīz’s heart, prompting him to commend Joseph to his household.
rows.anchor: فأوصى به أهله ذكره القشيري. وقد ذكر القولين في اسمها الثعلبي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies Quṭayfir as the king’s minister, serving al-Rayyān ibn al-Walīd; other accounts name al-Walīd ibn al-Rayyān, a giant, or Pharaoh of Moses.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: إنما اشتراه قطفير وزير ملك مصر، وهو الريان بن الوليد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Pharaoh identification is supported by Moses’ statement that Joseph had brought clear proofs to his people; another view makes Moses’ Pharaoh a descendant of Joseph’s Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو فرعون موسى لقول موسى: ولقد جآءكم يوسف من قبل بالبينات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account says Moses’ Pharaoh lived four hundred years; another says he descended from Joseph’s Pharaoh, with the latter claim deferred to the discussion of Sūrat Ghāfir.
rows.anchor: وأنه عاش أربعمائة سنة. وقيل: فرعون موسى من أولاد فرعون يوسف، على ما يأتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ʿAzīz oversaw the royal treasuries and bought Joseph from Mālik ibn Daʿr for twenty dinars, a garment, and two shoes; other accounts say the caravan sold him or that bidding rose dramatically.
rows.anchor: وكان هذا العزيز الذي اشترى يوسف على خزائن الملك واشترى يوسف من مالك بن دعر بعشرين دينارا، وزاده حلة ونعلين.

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: Wahb reports a fantastical auction: Joseph’s price rose to multiples of his weight in musk, amber, silk, gold, pearls, and jewels before Quṭayfir bought him.
rows.anchor: قاله وهب بن منبه. وقال وهب أيضا وغيره: ولما اشترى مالك بن دعر يوسف

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: Wahb says Mālik wrote a sale contract with Jacob’s sons for twenty dirhams, stipulating that Joseph was a runaway and must be taken chained and bound; the brothers guaranteed this condition.
rows.anchor: وقال وهب أيضا وغيره: ولما اشترى مالك بن دعر يوسف من إخوته كتب بينهم وبينه كتابا:

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: Wahb’s story has Joseph bid farewell to the brothers, praying for God to preserve, aid, and show mercy to them despite their betrayal; the sheep miscarried blood at the farewell.
rows.anchor: قاله وهب بن منبه. وقال وهب أيضا وغيره: ولما اشترى مالك بن دعر يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story describes chained Joseph embracing his mother’s grave, being beaten by a guard, and praying through his forefathers; Gabriel arrives amid cosmic darkness and dust, then Joseph forgives the guard and the world brightens.
rows.anchor: فمر على مقبرة آل كنعان فرأى قبر أمه وقد كان وكل به أسود يحرسه

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: In the same report the caravan leader confronts the guard, asks Joseph whether to retaliate or forgive, and Joseph chooses forgiveness hoping God will forgive him.
rows.anchor: قاله وهب بن منبه. وقال وهب أيضا وغيره: ولما اشترى مالك بن دعر يوسف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The account says the trader honored Joseph on the journey; at Egypt he bathed in the Nile, regained his beauty, and was sold in the city to Quṭayfir, the king’s minister.
rows.anchor: فاشتراه قطفير وزير الملك قاله ابن عباس على ما تقدم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One report says the king believed and followed Joseph’s religion before dying; the unbelieving Qābūs succeeded him, and Joseph invited him to Islam, which he refused.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن هذا الملك لم يمت حتى آمن واتبع يوسف على دينه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Honor his lodging” means treat Joseph’s residence and stay well with good food and fine clothing; mathwā derives from dwelling or remaining in a place.
rows.anchor: { أكرمي مثواه } أي منزله ومقامه بطيب المطعم واللباس الحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Perhaps he will benefit us” means Joseph may take care of some tasks when he grows up.
rows.anchor: { عسى أن ينفعنآ } أي يكفينا بعض المهمات إذا بلغ.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وابن إسحق
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Isḥāq say Quṭayfir was unable to father children, explaining his hope to adopt Joseph.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: كان حصورا لا يولد له، وكذا قال ابن إسحق:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adoption and enslavement seem contradictory, but the ʿAzīz could first free Joseph and then adopt him; adoption was known among earlier peoples and in early Islam.
rows.anchor: يعتقه ثم يتخذه ولدا بالتبني وكان التبني في الأمم معلوما عندهم

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd names three people of remarkable insight: the ʿAzīz about Joseph, Shuʿayb’s daughter about Moses, and Abū Bakr in appointing ʿUmar.
rows.anchor: أحسن الناس فراسة ثلاثة العزيز حين تفرس في يوسف

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabī objects that Abū Bakr chose ʿUmar through experience and companionship, while Shuʿayb’s daughter had clear evidence; neither case was extraordinary insight.
rows.anchor: قال ابن العربي: عجبا للمفسرين في اتفاقهم على جلب هذا الخبر

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Only the ʿAzīz’s assessment of Joseph may count as insight, since he had no outward sign; the author closes by conceding that point may be so.
rows.anchor: وأما أمر العزيز فيمكن أن يجعل فراسة لأنه لم يكن معه علامة ظاهرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurṭubī links God’s teaching Joseph dream interpretation to Jacob’s earlier prediction in the sixth verse; another report says God enabled Joseph to receive divine speech and interpret it.
rows.anchor:
ويعلمك من تأويل الأحاديث
[يوسف: 6].

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s enabling Joseph and teaching him interpretation fulfills Jacob’s earlier prediction; some understand the teaching as divine speech, interpretation, and dream interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المعنى مكناه لنوحي إليه بكلام منا، ونعلمه تأويله وتفسيره،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “God is dominant over His affair” may refer to God, whom nothing overcomes, or to Joseph, whom God directs and protects from hostile schemes.
rows.anchor: الهاء راجعة إلى الله تعالى أي لا يغلب الله شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Most people do not know” may mean people do not see the unseen, that everyone lacks unseen knowledge, or that selected people learn some of it; another reading targets disbelievers in divine decree.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المراد بالأكثر الجميع لأن أحدا لا يعلم الغيب.

rows.speaker: الحكماء
rows.claim: The sages illustrate God’s overriding plan: Jacob’s warning did not prevent Joseph telling the dream, the brothers’ plot led to Joseph’s rule, and the brothers’ effort to displace him deepened Jacob’s longing.
rows.anchor: حيث أمره يعقوب ألا يقص رؤياه على إخوته فغلب أمر الله حتى قص

rows.speaker: الحكماء
rows.claim: Their examples continue: the brothers failed to trick Jacob with tears and the shirt; the ʿAzīz ordered his wife to seek forgiveness, and the cupbearer forgot Joseph’s plea, prolonging prison.
rows.anchor: ثم أرادوا أن يخدعوا أباهم بالبكاء والقميص فغلب أمر الله

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh treats ashudd as a plural whose singular is shiddah.
rows.anchor: «أشده» عند سيبويه جمع، واحده شدة.

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī gives shadd as the singular, citing a line that describes the middle of the day.
rows.anchor: وقال الكسائي: واحده شد كما قال الشاعر:

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayd says Arabic has no singular form from the same word; ashudd means full strength before decline begins.
rows.anchor: وزعم أبو عبيد أنه لا واحد له من لفظه عند العرب

rows.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة
rows.claim: Mujāhid and Qatāda define reaching ashudd as age thirty-three.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد وقتادة: الأشد ثلاث وثلاثون سنة.

rows.speaker: ربيعة وزيد بن أسلم ومالك بن أنس
rows.claim: Rabīʿa, Zayd ibn Aslam, and Mālik ibn Anas define ashudd as reaching puberty.
rows.anchor: وقال ربيعة وزيد بن أسلم ومالك بن أنس: الأشد بلوغ الحلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We gave him judgment and knowledge” is variously explained as authority to judge, intellect and understanding with prophethood, prophethood and religious knowledge, or dream interpretation; childhood-prophethood proponents say knowledge increased at maturity.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: العقل والفهم والنبوة.

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says the general promise to reward every doer of good is aimed here at Muhammad: God will rescue him from hostile Meccans and establish him as He did Joseph.
rows.anchor: وقال الطبري: هذا وإن كان مخرجه ظاهرا على كل محسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The woman is the ʿAzīz’s wife; she sought sexual relations with Joseph. Murāwadah is gentle, patient seeking or requesting.
rows.anchor: وهي امرأة العزيز، طلبت منه أن يواقعها. وأصل المراودة الإرادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The intensive form ghallaqat suits repeated locking, unlike aghlaqa, which can describe many or few; one report says she locked seven doors.
rows.anchor: { وغلقت الأبواب } غلق للكثير، ولا يقال: غلق الباب وأغلق

rows.speaker: الفرزدق
rows.claim: Al-Farazdaq’s line about opening and closing doors witnesses the use of aghlaqa.
rows.anchor: ما زلت أغلق أبوابا وأفتحها حتى أتيت أبا عمرو بن عمار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hīt means “come here” or “approach”; it has no verbal noun or conjugation.
rows.anchor: أي هلم وأقبل وتعال ولا مصدر له ولا تصريف

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: A soundly transmitted reading from Ibn Masʿūd has hīt with open hāʾ and tāʾ; he says he recites as taught and explains it as “come” or “approach.”
rows.anchor: عن أبي وائل قال: سمعت عبد الله بن مسعود يقرأ «هيت لك»

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وسعيد بن جبير والحسن ومجاهد وعكرمة وأبو عمرو وعاصم والأعمش وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, ʿIkrima, and these named reciters read hīt with both vowels open.
rows.anchor: وهذه القراءة بفتح التاء والهاء هي الصحيحة من قراءة ابن عباس وسعيد بن جبير

rows.speaker: ابن أبي إسحق
rows.claim: Ibn Abī Isḥāq reads the word with open hāʾ and kasra on tāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن أبي إسحق النحوي «قالت هيت لك» بفتح الهاء وكسر التاء

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الرحمن السلمي وابن كثير
rows.claim: Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī and Ibn Kathīr read with open hāʾ and ḍamma on tāʾ; Ṭarafa’s poem attests this pronunciation.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عبد الرحمن السلمي وابن كثير «هيت لك» بفتح الهاء وضم التاء

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر وشيبة ونافع
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar, Shayba, and Nāfiʿ read hīt with kasra on hāʾ and fatḥa on tāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر وشيبة ونافع «وقالت هيت لك» بكسر الهاء وفتح التاء.

rows.speaker: يحيى بن وثاب وعلي بن أبي طالب وابن عباس ومجاهد وعكرمة
rows.claim: Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb has kasra, a silent yāʾ, and ḍamma on tāʾ; reports from ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and ʿIkrima have a hamza and ḍamma on tāʾ.
rows.anchor: وروي عن علي بن أبي طالب رضي الله عنه وابن عباس ومجاهد وعكرمة: «وقالت هئت لك»

rows.speaker: ابن عامر وأهل الشام
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir and Syrian readers use the hamza form with kasra on hāʾ and fatḥa on tāʾ; Abū Jaʿfar explains the vowel variants through pause and meeting-sukun rules.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عامر وأهل الشام: «وقالت هئت» بكسر الهاء وبالهمزة وبفتح التاء

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: For the hamza form, fatḥa eases two adjacent sukūns, kasra follows the default movement of a sakin, and ḍamma signals an implied possessive meaning such as “my invitation to you.”
rows.anchor: قال أبو جعفر: «هئت لك» بفتح التاء لالتقاء الساكنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Medinan reading may instead derive from hāʾa/yahīʾu: hīʾtu means “I became ready/beautiful for you,” with lak as a separate phrase; other hamza readings mean “I prepared myself for you.”
rows.anchor: والآخر أن يكون فعلا من هاء يهيء مثل جاء يجيء

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr rejects the hamza-and-ḍamma reading as false, challenging its supporters to find Arabs who use it.
rows.anchor: أنكر أبو عمرو هذه القراءة قال أبو عبيدة معمر بن المثنى

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī also says the form hīʾtu is not attested from Arab usage; ʿIkrima’s “I prepared and adorned myself” gloss is therefore deemed unsatisfactory.
rows.anchor: وقال الكسائي أيضا: لم تحك «هئت» عن العرب.

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Naḥḥās considers the reading good by Basran grammar, deriving it from hāʾa yahīʾu as in jāʾa yajīʾu.
rows.anchor: قال النحاس: وهي جيدة عند البصريين لأنه يقال: هاء الرجل يهاء

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj prefers the open-hāʾ/open-tāʾ reading, supported by Ṭarafa’s line.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: أجود القراءات «هيت» بفتح الهاء والتاء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan say hīt is a Syriac word inviting the woman to herself; al-Suddī calls it a Coptic form meaning “come here.”
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس والحسن: «هيت» كلمة بالسريانية تدعوه إلى نفسها.

rows.speaker: الكسائي وأبو عبيد وعكرمة
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī says it is a Hauran dialect meaning “come,” confirmed by a learned Hauran man; Abū ʿUbayd and ʿIkrima report this explanation.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيد: فسألت شيخا عالما من حوران فذكر أنها لغتهم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid and others regard hīt as an Arabic call to the woman, an urging to come; al-Jawharī cites related verbs and poems meaning to shout or summon.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد وغيره: هي لغة عربية تدعوه بها إلى نفسها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maʿādh Allāh is an omitted verb with its verbal noun in the accusative; the noun is annexed to God as an object, like an idiom meaning “as I passed by ʿAmr.”
rows.anchor: أي أعوذ بالله وأستجير به مما دعوتني إليه وهو مصدر

rows.speaker: مجاهد وابن إسحق والسدي
rows.claim: Mujāhid, Ibn Isḥāq, and al-Suddī take “he is my lord” to mean her husband, Joseph’s master, whom Joseph will not betray after his kindness.
rows.anchor: يعني زوجها، أي هو سيدي أكرمني فلا أخونه قاله مجاهد وابن إسحق والسدي.

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj instead reads “my lord” as God, who cared for Joseph, so Joseph will not commit what God forbids.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: أي إن الله ربي تولاني بلطفه، فلا أركب ما حرمه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reported dialogue has Joseph refuse praise of his looks by pointing to God’s creation and the body’s decay, refuse to look at her for fear of afterlife blindness, and reject privacy or luxurious bedding because God sees him.
rows.anchor: قال: في الرحم صورني ربي قالت: يا يوسف ما أحسن شعرك!

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetes agree the wife intended sin; they differ over Joseph’s desire. The author’s preferred reading is that the proof prevented any sinful intention, required by prophetic impeccability, with the clause understood in inverted order.
rows.anchor: واختلف العلماء في همه ولا خلاف أن همها كان المعصية

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda interprets the clause by antecedent and postponed wording: she desired him, and absent his seeing his Lord’s proof, he would have desired her.
rows.anchor: هذا على التقديم والتأخير كأنه أراد ولقد همت به ولولا أن رأى برهان ربه

rows.speaker: أحمد بن يحيى
rows.claim: Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā distinguishes the two desires: the wife was resolved on sin, while Joseph’s desire did not lead him to commit what he had considered.
rows.anchor: وقال أحمد بن يحيى: أي همت زليخاء بالمعصية وكانت مصرة، وهم يوسف ولم يواقع ما هم به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited poems use hamm as an uncompleted inward thought, without resolve.
rows.anchor: فهذا كله حديث نفس من غير عزم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other interpretations say Joseph wished to marry her, or intended to strike/push her away; the latter says the proof prevented an act that might falsely suggest sexual intent.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هم بها تمنى زوجيتها. وقيل: هم بها أي بضربها ودفعها

rows.speaker: جمهور المفسرين
rows.claim: Most exegetes reportedly take Joseph’s desire as sinful and say he sat in a sexual posture; this is supported by reports attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, and Mujāhid.
rows.anchor: وإلى هذا القول ذهب معظم المفسرين وعامتهم، فيما ذكر القشيري أبو نصر،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to say Joseph loosened his waist tie and sat between her legs, with another report describing him removing his clothes.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: حل الهميان وجلس منها مجلس الخاتن،

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير ومجاهد
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says Joseph released his trousers’ tie; Mujāhid says he lowered his trousers and sat as a man does with his wife.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن جبير: أطلق تكة سراويله. وقال مجاهد: حل السراويل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report links Joseph’s later “I did not betray him in his absence” to Gabriel asking whether he had not desired the wife, after which Joseph said he did not absolve himself.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: ولما قال: ذلك ليعلم أني لم أخنه بالغيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author explains the analogy to “if you knew with certainty”: its omitted response would be that people would not compete for worldly goods.
rows.anchor: وجوابه لم تتنافسوا قال ابن عطية:

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وجماعة من السلف
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and early authorities reportedly say the story offers sinners hope that repentance can win pardon and that nearness to sin need not ruin a person.
rows.anchor: روي هذا القول عن ابن عباس وجماعة من السلف

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد القاسم بن سلام
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayd says Ibn ʿAbbās and later authorities agree Joseph desired her; they knew God and scripture and honored prophets too highly to speak without knowledge.
rows.anchor: وابن عباس ومن دونه لا يختلفون في أنه هم بها

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says God recounts prophets’ sins to keep people from despairing of repentance, not to shame the prophets.
rows.anchor: إن الله عز وجل لم يذكر معاصي الأنبياء ليعيرهم بها

rows.speaker: الغزنوي
rows.claim: Al-Ghaznawī lists wisdom in prophetic slips: greater fear and shame, relinquishing pride in deeds, savoring forgiveness, and giving sinners examples of hope.
rows.anchor: قال الغزنوي: مع أن لزلة الأنبياء حكما: زيادة الوجل، وشدة الحياء

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: Al-Qushayrī says Joseph experienced a natural impulse without settled resolve; because the proof diverted it, it was like a fasting person merely thinking of water or food.
rows.anchor: كان ذلك الهم حركة طبع من غير تصميم للعقد على الفعل

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya doubts that Joseph was a prophet at the time and allows an intention or lingering bad thought without action; if he was already a prophet, only an involuntary passing thought is possible.
rows.anchor: إن كون يوسف نبيا في وقت هذه النازلة لم يصح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author accepts Ibn ʿAṭiyya’s distinction but rejects his denial of Joseph’s prophethood: God’s revelation to Joseph proves he was a prophet, so only an unchosen thought, not settled intention, remains possible.
rows.anchor: قلت: ما ذكره من هذا التفصيل صحيح لكن قوله تعالى: { وأوحينا إليه } يدل على

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph knew that adultery, its preliminaries, and betraying a master or neighbor were forbidden, and acted on that knowledge by refusing the wife and fleeing.
rows.anchor: فقد عمل يوسف بما علمه الله من تحريم الزنى ومقدماته، وخيانة السيد

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, Abū Hurayra reports that angels are told to watch a servant who intends a sin: if he leaves it, God records a good deed because he left it for God.
rows.anchor: في صحيح مسلم عن أبي هريرة رضي الله عنه قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A second sound report says that when a servant intends a sin but does not do it, God records a good deed.
rows.anchor: إذا هم عبدي بسيئة فلم يعملها كتبت حسنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author reasons that abandoned sinful thought incurs no sin, citing the sound hadith that God forgives the community’s unspoken and unacted inner thoughts.
rows.anchor: إن الله تجاوز لأمتي عما حدثت به أنفسها ما لم تعمل أو تكلم به

rows.speaker: ابن عطاء
rows.claim: In Ibn al-ʿArabī’s story, a questioner asks whether Joseph desired but did not act; Ibn ʿAṭāʾ answers yes, because divine care was present, and the author praises their concise exchange.
rows.anchor: قال: نعم! لأن العناية من ثم. فانظر إلى حلاوة العالم والمتعلم

rows.speaker: علماء الصوفية
rows.claim: Sufi authorities say God gave Joseph judgment and knowledge just as sexual desire arose, making that gift a cause of his protection.
rows.anchor: إنما أعطاه ذلك إبان غلبة الشهوة لتكون له سببا للعصمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the story in which Sulaymān ibn Yasār ranks himself above Joseph: that would make sainthood higher than prophethood, and even a nonprophet Joseph would be protected.
rows.anchor: فإن هذا يقتضي أن تكون درجة الولاية أرفع من درجة النبوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “had he not seen his Lord’s proof,” an is nominative as “seeing”; the omitted response is clear to the listener.
rows.anchor: «أن» في موضع رفع أي لولا رؤية برهان ربه والجواب محذوف لعلم السامع

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: ʿAlī reports that the wife covered her jeweled idol before approaching Joseph; he replied that he should be more ashamed before God, and the author calls this the strongest explanation of the proof.
rows.anchor: روي عن علي بن أبي طالب رضي الله عنه أن زليخاء قامت إلى صنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reports say Joseph saw Qur’anic warnings written on the ceiling or a hand bearing the words “over you are guardians,” or remembered his covenant with God.
rows.anchor: وقيل: رأى مكتوبا في سقف البيت ولا تقربوا الزنى إنه كان فاحشة

rows.speaker: قتادة ومجاهد والحسن والضحاك وأبو صالح وسعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: These authorities say Joseph saw Jacob on the wall, biting a finger and threatening him; his desire then left his fingers.
rows.anchor: قاله قتادة ومجاهد والحسن والضحاك وأبو صالح وسعيد بن جبير.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid’s report says Joseph had loosened his trousers when Jacob appeared, and Joseph fled; another report says Jacob struck his chest and the desire left his fingers.
rows.anchor: روى الأعمش عن مجاهد قال: حل سراويله فتمثل له يعقوب،

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says Jacob’s sons each had twelve sons except Joseph, who had two, because the interrupted desire diminished his offspring.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: فولد لكل واحد من أولاد يعقوب اثنا عشر ذكرا إلا يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In general, the proof was a divine sign that strengthened Joseph’s faith and made him abstain from sin.
rows.anchor: فذلك البرهان آية من آيات الله أراها الله يوسف حتى قوي إيمانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūʾ and faḥshāʾ are variously glossed as desire and intercourse, bad reputation and adultery, betrayal and sexual sin, or punishment from the ʿAzīz.
rows.anchor: والسوء الشهوة، والفحشاء المباشرة.

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو عمرو وابن عامر
rows.claim: These reciters read al-mukhliṣīn with kasra on the lām, meaning those who devoted themselves to God; others use fatḥa, meaning those God selected for revelation, and Joseph had both qualities.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو وابن عامر «المخلصين» بكسر اللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The concise narrative implies that Joseph fled after seeing the proof, the woman chased him to bring him back, and she caught him before he escaped.
rows.anchor: وهذا من اختصار القرآن المعجز الذي يجتمع فيه المعاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: She tore his shirt from behind, catching its upper part so the tear ran down from the collar; qadd usually means a lengthwise cut, while qaṭṭ is across.
rows.anchor: قبضت في أعلى قميصه فتخرق القميص عند طوقه

rows.speaker: النابغة
rows.claim: Al-Nābigha’s verse about the layered armor witnesses qadd as a lengthwise cut.
rows.anchor: تقد السلوقي المضاعف نسجه وتوقد بالصفاح نار الحباحب

rows.speaker: المفضل بن حرب
rows.claim: Al-Mufaḍḍal ibn Ḥarb says a codex had ʿaṭṭa instead of quddat, meaning “was torn”; Yaʿqūb says ʿaṭṭ is a tear in sound skin or cloth.
rows.anchor: وقال المفضل بن حرب: قرأت في مصحف «فلما رأى قميصه عط من دبر» أي شق.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse supports reasoning from customary signs: a garment usually tears where it is pulled, front or back, a principle the author says the Mālikīs uniquely discuss.
rows.anchor: الثانية: في الآية دليل على القياس والاعتبار، والعمل بالعرف والعادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sayyid refers to the ʿAzīz, her husband; Egyptians call a husband a lord. Alfāhu means found him, with several synonymous verbs.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: { وألفيا سيدها لدى الباب } أي وجدا العزيز عند الباب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wife alleges Joseph sought adultery and proposes prison or painful punishment; grammatically “or punishment” may also be accusative, meaning he should be punished.
rows.anchor: ف { قالت ما جزآء من أراد بأهلك سوءا } أي زنى.

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī allows reading “or painful punishment” in the accusative, with an implied verb meaning “or he be punished.”
rows.anchor: ويجوز أو عذابا أليما بمعنى: أو يعذب عذابا أليما قاله الكسائي.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because a lover favors the beloved, the wife could not truthfully claim Joseph loved her; he therefore answers her false accusation with the truth that she solicited him.
rows.anchor: لما برأت نفسها ولم تكن صادقة في حبه

rows.speaker: نوف الشامي
rows.claim: Nawf al-Shāmī and others say Joseph did not initially expose the affair; he spoke plainly only after she slandered him.
rows.anchor: قال نوف الشامي وغيره: كأن يوسف عليه السلام لم يبن عن كشف القضية،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The witness from her family is a judge or arbiter, not necessarily a testimonial witness: their conflicting claims required a way to identify the truthful speaker.
rows.anchor: أي حكم حاكم من أهلها لأنه حكم منه وليس بشهادة

rows.speaker: السهيلي والقشيري
rows.claim: One view makes the witness an infant who spoke in the cradle; al-Suhaylī calls this correct based on a Prophetic report, and al-Qushayrī says the child was her maternal uncle’s son.
rows.anchor: الأول أنه طفل في المهد تكلم قال السهيلي: وهو الصحيح للحديث الوارد فيه عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم،

rows.speaker: ابن أبي نجيح عن مجاهد
rows.claim: A second view, transmitted by Ibn Abī Najīḥ from Mujāhid, makes the witness Joseph’s shirt: its condition spoke eloquently, as Arabic often attributes speech to objects.
rows.anchor: أن الشاهد قد القميص رواه ابن أبي نجيح عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: A third view says the witness was a being neither human nor jinn; the author says “from her family” rules this out.
rows.anchor: أنه خلق من خلق الله تعالى ليس بإنسي ولا بجني قاله مجاهد

rows.speaker: الحسن وعكرمة وقتادة والضحاك ومجاهد والسدي
rows.claim: A fourth view makes him a wise man in the household who inferred the truth from the shirt’s direction of tearing; al-Suddī says he was her cousin, a view also related from Ibn ʿAbbās.
rows.anchor: وكان من جملة أهل المرأة، وكان مع زوجها فقال: قد سمعت الاستدبار والجلبة

rows.speaker: عكرمة ومجاهد
rows.claim: ʿIkrima and Mujāhid say the witness was an adult wise man; Sufyān transmits Mujāhid’s report that he was a man.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة: لم يكن بصبي، ولكن كان رجلا حكيما.

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Naḥḥās thinks an adult counselor is likelier: a speaking infant’s words would themselves be a miraculous proof, making ordinary evidence from the shirt unnecessary.
rows.anchor: والأشبه بالمعنى والله أعلم أن يكون رجلا عاقلا حكيما

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: He reconciles the hadith calling the witness one of four “small” speakers by taking ṣaghīr to mean young, not elderly; he also notes reports that Ibn ʿAbbās said the witness was not a child.
rows.anchor: منهم صاحب يوسف يكون المعنى: صغيرا ليس بشيخ وفي هذا دليل آخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Hurayra, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Hilāl ibn Yasāf, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk instead make the witness a cradle infant; the author argues that the child’s speech alone would be miraculous proof.
rows.anchor: قد روي عن ابن عباس وأبي هريرة وابن جبير وهلال بن يساف والضحاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the witness was a child, the episode does not establish legal use of circumstantial signs; if an adult, the verse supports decisions from indicators, as in property disputes.
rows.anchor: إذا تنزلنا على أن يكون الشاهد طفلا صغيرا فلا يكون فيه دلالة

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik says that when thieves possess disputed goods and claimants lack formal proof, the authority waits; if no competing claimant appears, the goods may be handed to them.
rows.anchor: حتى قال مالك في اللصوص: إذا وجدت معهم أمتعة فجاء قوم فادعوها،

rows.speaker: محمد
rows.claim: Muḥammad says in household property disputes, men’s items belong to the man, women’s to the woman, and shared items to the man; Shurayḥ and Iyās also judged by indicators.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد في متاع البيت إذا اختلفت فيه المرأة والرجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional kāna is grammatically explained as a strong verb serving for all actions, or as “if it is known,” so its past form describes an as-yet-unrealized condition.
rows.anchor: لأن حروف الشرط ترد الماضي إلى المستقبل، وليس هذا في كان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar and Ibn Abī Isḥāq read qabl and dubr as terminal adverbs with suppressed possessors; other readers use diptote-like fatḥa or shortened genitive forms.
rows.anchor: وقرأ يحيى بن يعمر وابن أبي إسحق «من قبل» بضم القاف والباء واللام، وكذا «دبر»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say the ʿAzīz said “this is your cunning” after hearing her accusation; others attribute the words to the witness.
rows.anchor: قيل: قال لها ذلك العزيز عند قولها: «ما جزاء من أراد بأهلك سوءا».

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kayd means plotting or deception, discussed earlier in Sūrat al-Anfāl.
rows.anchor: والكيد: المكر والحيلة، وقد تقدم في «الأنفال».

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He calls the women’s plotting great because of its severe temptation and their skill at escaping their predicament.
rows.anchor: وإنما قال «عظيم» لعظم فتنتهن واحتيالهن في التخلص من ورطتهن.

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A report attributed through Abū Hurayra to the Prophet compares women’s plotting with Satan’s, citing the Qur’anic statements that Satan’s plot is weak and the women’s plot great; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل عن يحيى بن أبي كثير عن أبي هريرة قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم:

rows.speaker: الشاهد
rows.claim: The witness tells Joseph to turn away from the incident, meaning to keep it private and not tell anyone.
rows.anchor: القائل هذا هو الشاهد. و«يوسف» نداء مفرد، أي يا يوسف، فحذف.

rows.speaker: الشاهد
rows.claim: The witness then tells the wife to seek her husband’s forgiveness for her sin so he will not punish her.
rows.anchor: ثم أقبل عليها فقال: وأنت { واستغفري لذنبك } يقول: استغفري زوجك من ذنبك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The masculine plural khāṭiʾīn includes women through masculine grammatical agreement, or means “the people who err”; Qur’an uses the same pattern elsewhere.
rows.anchor: ولم يقل من الخاطئات لأنه قصد الإخبار عن المذكر والمؤنث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says the husband was not jealous, as was common among many Egyptians; another says God removed his jealousy as a kindness that spared Joseph the husband’s retaliation.
rows.anchor: أنه لم يكن غيورا فلذلك كان ساكنا

rows.speaker: الأعمش والمفضل والسلمي
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash, al-Mufaḍḍal, and al-Sulamī read niswah with ḍamma on nūn; nisāʾ is the larger plural, and both feminine and masculine verb agreement occur.
rows.anchor: ويقال: «نسوة» بضم النون، وهي قراءة الأعمش والمفضل والسلمي، والجمع الكثير نساء.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story spread among Egyptian women; they may have included wives of the cupbearer, baker, animal keeper, and jailer, or the doorkeeper’s wife according to Ibn ʿAbbās and others.
rows.anchor: قيل: امرأة ساقي العزيز، وامرأة خبازه، وامرأة صاحب دوابه، وامرأة صاحب سجنه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fatā in Arabic means a young man; its feminine is fatāt.
rows.anchor: { تراود فتاها عن نفسه } الفتى في كلام العرب الشاب، والمرأة فتاة.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: “It entered her shighāf” is glossed by Mujāhid as the love penetrating her heart’s covering; a report from Ibn ʿAbbās via ʿIkrima says it entered beneath it.
rows.anchor: وقيل: دخل حبه في شغافها عن مجاهد وغيره.

rows.speaker: الحسن والسدي وأبو عبيد
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan calls shighāf the heart’s interior; al-Suddī and Abū ʿUbayd call it the heart’s enclosing membrane, with other explanations naming its middle.
rows.anchor: السدي وأبو عبيد: شغاف القلب غلافه، وهو جلدة عليه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These explanations converge on love reaching and overpowering the heart; a line by al-Nābigha compares penetration to fingers entering a heart’s covering.
rows.anchor: والمعنى في هذه الأقوال متقارب، والمعنى: وصل حبه إلى شغافها فغلب عليه

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر بن محمد وابن محيصن والحسن
rows.claim: These readers use shaʿaf with unpointed ʿayn, glossed as burning the heart; al-Jawharī says shaʿaf al-ḥubb means love burned his heart, and Abū Zayd says it made him ill.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر بن محمد وابن محيصن والحسن «شعفها» بالعين غير معجمة

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbī distinguishes shaghaf, love, from shaʿaf, madness; al-Ḥasan separately says shighāf is the heart’s cover and shaʿāf its innermost substance.
rows.anchor: وروي عن الشعبي أنه قال: الشغف بالغين المعجمة حب، والشعف بالعين غير المعجمة جنون.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says “her young man” was her husband’s servant, since Joseph was legally treated as a slave and had to carry out her orders.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: «فتاها» وهو فتى زوجها، لأن يوسف كان عندهم في حكم المماليك،

rows.speaker: سلمان الفارسي
rows.claim: A report from Salmān says the wife obtained Joseph from her husband by claiming she would adopt him, raised him to adulthood while desiring him, then tried to seduce him; God protected him.
rows.anchor: إن امرأة العزيز استوهبت زوجها يوسف فوهبه لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wife heard the women gossiping and plotting to shame her; another explanation says she had entrusted them with her secret and they betrayed it.
rows.anchor: أي بغيبتهن إياها، واحتيالهن في ذمها.

rows.speaker: مجاهد عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Mujāhid transmits Ibn ʿAbbās’s account that she told her husband she wanted to invite the women to a meal, and he agreed.
rows.anchor: فقال مجاهد عن ابن عباس: إن امرأة العزيز قالت لزوجها إني أريد أن أتخذ طعاما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The text omits that she invited them to a banquet designed to expose them to the same temptation; she decorated the rooms and instructed every named woman to attend.
rows.anchor: في الكلام حذف أي أرسلت إليهن تدعوهن إلى وليمة لتوقعهن فيما وقعت فيه

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: Wahb says forty women came reluctantly; a line attributed to Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt describes their forced arrival and prepared couches and carpets.
rows.anchor: قال وهب بن منبه: إنهن كن أربعين امرأة فجئن على كره منهن،

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr says each seat had a cup of honey, a citron, and a sharp knife.
rows.anchor: قال ابن جبير: في كل مجلس جام فيه عسل وأترج وسكين حاد.

rows.speaker: مجاهد وسعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Mujāhid and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr read mutka without hamza and with a shortened form, explaining it as citron in Coptic; Mujāhid distinguishes heavy muttaka as food.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد وسعيد بن جبير: «متكا» مخففا غير مهموز، والمتك هو الأترج

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Naḥḥās argues that the knife detail supports an implied food: the women carried knives to cut food, as the omitted phrase “food for reclining” may suggest.
rows.anchor: ودل على هذا الحذف «وآتت كل واحدة منهن سكينا» لأن حضور النساء معهن سكاكين إنما هو لطعام يقطع بالسكاكين كذا قال في كتاب «إعراب القرآن» له.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Maʿmar transmits Qatāda’s explanation of muttaka as food; another view takes it as anything reclined on during a meal, drink, or conversation.
rows.anchor: وروى معمر عن قتادة قال: «المتكأ» الطعام.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qutbī says “we reclined at someone’s place” can mean “we ate”; the word derives from mawtakaʾ, like forms derived from “weighed,” “promised,” and “leaned.”
rows.anchor: وحكى القتبي أنه يقال: اتكأنا عند فلان أي أكلنا، والأصل في «متكأ» موتكأ،

rows.speaker: الكسائي والفراء
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ say sakīn may be masculine or feminine; al-Farrāʾ cites a masculine form, while al-Aṣmaʿī recognizes only masculine usage.
rows.anchor: وحكى الكسائي والفراء أن السكين يذكر ويؤنث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb’s tāʾ in “she said, come out” has ḍamma to ease two adjacent sukūns; kasra follows the original form.
rows.anchor: بضم التاء لالتقاء الساكنين لأن الكسرة تثقل إذا كان بعدها ضمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A story says she told the women not to cut or eat until she instructed them, then called Joseph by saying “Iel”; the account calls Iel their idol and also gives a Hebrew gloss “the Lord.”
rows.anchor: وكان يوسف عليه السلام يعمل في الطين، وقد شد مئزره، وحسر عن ذراعيه

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: Wahb says the women cut their hands with blades to the bone; Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says Joseph entered unexpectedly after being adorned, and the women mistook citron for their hands.
rows.anchor: بالمدى حتى بلغت السكاكين إلى العظم قاله وهب بن منبه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One report from Ibn ʿAbbās explains akbarnahu as magnifying and revering Joseph; another says the women emitted fluids from astonishment.
rows.anchor: أعظمنه وهبنه وعنه أيضا أمنين وأمذين من الدهش

rows.speaker: ابن سمعان
rows.claim: Ibn Samʿān transmits from several people that the women experienced sexual fluids out of intense infatuation.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن سمعان عن عدة من أصحابه: إنهم قالوا أمذين عشقا

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: Wahb says ten women died in the gathering from bewilderment, longing, and astonishment at Joseph.
rows.anchor: وهب بن منبه: عشقنه حتى مات منهن عشرة في ذلك المجلس دهشا وحيرة

rows.speaker: قتادة ومقاتل والسدي
rows.claim: Qatāda, Muqātil, and al-Suddī interpret akbarnahu as menstruating from shock and cite a poem; Abū ʿUbayda rejects this lexical meaning, though shock can cause bleeding.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه حضن من الدهش قاله قتادة ومقاتل والسدي قال الشاعر:

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says akbarnahu cannot itself mean “they menstruated,” since Arabic says akbarat, not the proposed verbal gloss.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: يقال أكبرنه، ولا يقال حضنه،

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azharī answers that menstruation could be called akbartu because a girl passes from childhood into adulthood when her period begins.
rows.anchor: وأجاب الأزهري فقال: يجوز أكبرت بمعنى حاضت

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī offers a stronger alternative: the feminine hāʾ may refer to the verbal noun, “they menstruated a menstruation”; treating it as a pause hāʾ is unsound because it should disappear in connected speech.
rows.anchor: وأمثل منه قول ابن الأنباري: إن الهاء كناية عن مصدر الفعل،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥāshā li-llāh means “God forbid”; Nāfiʿ reportedly reads ḥāshā with a final alif, its original form, while omission treats li-llāh as its replacement.
rows.anchor: أي معاذ الله. وروى الأصمعي عن نافع أنه قرأ كما قرأ أبو عمرو بن العلاء.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression has four forms, with either a pronoun or prepositional phrase; it can take a genitive or accusative complement.
rows.anchor: وفيها أربع لغات يقال: حاشاك وحاشا لك وحاش لك وحشا لك.

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad prefers construing ḥāshā as a verb and taking its complement in the accusative; the poem by al-Nābigha and an Arab’s invocation are cited as evidence.
rows.anchor: قال النحاس: وسمعت علي بن سليمان يقول سمعت محمد بن يزيد يقول: النصب أولى لأنه قد صح أنها فعل

rows.speaker: الحسن وابن مسعود وأبي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan reads with a still šīn or “ḥāsha the God”; Ibn Masʿūd and Ubayy read “ḥāsha God” without li, supported by a poetic citation.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن «وقلن حاش لله» بإسكان الشين،

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj derives the word from the outskirts: ḥāshā li-Zayd means Zayd stood apart from a charge, while exception removes someone from a mentioned group.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: وأصل الكلمة من الحاشية، والحشا بمعنى الناحية،

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī treats ḥāshā as a verb of exclusion, placing Joseph apart from the accusation or from being human; Sibawayh treats it as a preposition, while al-Mubarrad and Abū ʿAlī take it as a verb.
rows.anchor: هو فاعل من المحاشاة أي حاشا يوسف وصار في حاشية وناحية

rows.speaker: الخليل وسيبويه
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl and Sībawayh treat mā as equivalent to laysa, so “this is not a human” takes the accusative; the Kufan analysis preserves the case of an omitted preposition, which al-Naḥḥās rejects as inconsistent.
rows.anchor: قال الخليل وسيبويه: «ما» بمنزلة ليس تقول: ليس زيد قائما، و«ما هذا بشرا»
